Pathology-04.question: ১) A positive tuberculin test signifies which type of immunity?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is T-cell mediated immunity. A positive tuberculin (Mantoux) test indicates a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction (Type IV hypersensitivity) mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes (mainly Th1 cells).

When tuberculin antigen is injected, memory T cells release cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ), causing macrophage activation and local induration.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • B-cell mediated – Involves antibody-mediated (humoral) immunity.

  • Complement mediated – Part of innate and antibody-mediated immune responses, not responsible for Mantoux reaction.

  • Phagocyte mediated – Macrophages participate in the reaction, but the initiating mechanism is T-cell mediated.

High-yield points:

Tuberculin (Mantoux) test:

  • Type → Type IV hypersensitivity

  • Mediator → T lymphocytes (Th1 cells)

  • Onset → 48–72 hours

  • Response → Induration due to macrophage infiltration

Exam pearl:
Positive Mantoux test = Cell-mediated immunity = T cells.

Pathology-04.question: ২) Which of the following disease, total lung capacity is greatly increased?
৩) Secondary pulmonary tuberculosis involves which area of lung?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is apex of the lung. Secondary (post-primary) pulmonary tuberculosis typically affects the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes, especially due to the higher oxygen tension in these regions, which favours growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Base – More commonly involved in aspiration-related conditions, not secondary TB.

  • Lower lobe – Not the typical site of secondary TB.

  • Middle lobe – Not the characteristic location.

High-yield points:

Types of pulmonary TB:

Type Common site
Primary TB Lower part of upper lobe or upper part of lower lobe (Ghon focus)
Secondary TB Apex of upper lobe
Miliary TB Multiple organs via hematogenous spread

Exam pearl:
Secondary pulmonary TB = Apical lesion (upper lobe apex).

Pathology-04.question: ৪) Most common extra-pulomanry site of TB is
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is lymph node. Tuberculous lymphadenitis is the most common form of extra-pulmonary tuberculosis, commonly involving the cervical lymph nodes (scrofula).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Intestine – Can be affected, especially in abdominal TB, but is less common.

  • Brain – TB meningitis is an important complication but not the most common extra-pulmonary site.

  • Bone – Osteoarticular TB occurs but is less frequent.

High-yield points:

Common extra-pulmonary TB sites:

  1. Lymph nodes (most common)

  2. Pleura

  3. Genitourinary tract

  4. Bones and joints

  5. CNS (TB meningitis)

Exam pearl:
Most common extra-pulmonary TB = Lymph node (cervical lymphadenitis).

Pathology-04.question: ৫) Which of the following is the most common cause of acute community-acquired pneumonia?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is the most common cause of acute community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in adults.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • S. aureus – Causes pneumonia, especially after influenza infection, in hospital settings, or in intravenous drug users.

  • K. pneumoniae – Causes pneumonia mainly in alcoholics, diabetics, and debilitated patients; classically produces "currant jelly" sputum.

  • L. pneumonia (Legionella) – Causes atypical pneumonia, often associated with contaminated water sources.

High-yield points:

Common CAP organisms:

  1. Streptococcus pneumoniae → most common

  2. Haemophilus influenzae

  3. Atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella)

  4. Viruses

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia = S. pneumoniae.

Pathology-04.question: ৬) Which of the following is the most common cause of hospital acquired pneumonia?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It is one of the most common causes of hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), especially in critically ill patients, ventilated patients, and those with prolonged hospital stay. It is associated with multidrug resistance.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • S. aureus – Important cause of HAP, particularly MRSA, but not the most common overall.

  • S. pneumoniae – Commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), not HAP.

  • K. pneumoniae – A common hospital pathogen, especially in ICU patients, but less common than Pseudomonas in HAP.

High-yield points:

Pneumonia organisms:

Type Most common organism
Community-acquired pneumonia S. pneumoniae
Hospital-acquired pneumonia P. aeruginosa (classically)
Ventilator-associated pneumonia Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, MRSA

Risk factors for Pseudomonas pneumonia:

  • Mechanical ventilation

  • ICU admission

  • Previous antibiotics

  • Structural lung disease (e.g., bronchiectasis)

Exam pearl:
HAP = Pseudomonas aeruginosa (classic exam answer).

Pathology-04.question: ৭) Which of the following is the most common cause of cancer related mortality worldwide?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is lung cancer. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide due to its high incidence, aggressive nature, and late presentation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Breast cancer – The most commonly diagnosed cancer in many women worldwide, but not the leading cause of cancer death overall.

  • Leukaemia – Important hematological malignancy but contributes fewer cancer deaths compared with lung cancer.

  • Gastric cancer – A major cause of cancer mortality, especially in some regions, but lower globally than lung cancer.

High-yield points:

Worldwide cancer facts:

  • Most common cause of cancer death → Lung cancer

  • Major risk factor → Smoking

  • Most common histological type → Adenocarcinoma (currently)

Exam pearl:
Cancer mortality worldwide = Lung cancer.

Pathology-04.question: ৮) Which of the following is the most common type of lung cancer in non-smokers?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is adenocarcinoma. Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in non-smokers and is also the most common overall histological type of lung cancer in many populations.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Squamous carcinoma – Strongly associated with smoking and usually arises centrally near bronchi.

  • Small cell carcinoma – Almost exclusively associated with smoking and has neuroendocrine features.

  • Large cell carcinoma – A less common type of non-small cell lung cancer.

High-yield points:

Lung cancer types:

Type Association
Adenocarcinoma Most common in non-smokers; peripheral lung lesion
Squamous cell carcinoma Smoking; central bronchus; PTHrP → hypercalcaemia
Small cell carcinoma Smoking; SIADH, Cushing syndrome, Lambert-Eaton syndrome
Large cell carcinoma Poorly differentiated NSCLC

Exam pearl:
Non-smoker with lung cancer → Adenocarcinoma.

Pathology-04.question: ৯) Persistent productive cough for at least 3 consecutive months in at least 2 consecutive years
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is chronic bronchitis. It is clinically defined as:

Persistent productive cough for ≥3 months in each of 2 consecutive years (after excluding other causes).

It is a form of COPD characterized by chronic mucus hypersecretion and airway inflammation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • COPD – A broader term that includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema, but the given definition specifically describes chronic bronchitis.

  • Emphysema – Characterized by destruction of alveolar walls and permanent enlargement of air spaces, not defined by chronic productive cough.

  • Bronchiectasis – Causes chronic productive cough due to irreversible bronchial dilatation, often with recurrent infections, but has a different diagnostic basis.

High-yield points:

COPD components:

  • Chronic bronchitis → "Blue bloater" → productive cough + mucus hypersecretion

  • Emphysema → "Pink puffer" → alveolar destruction + hyperinflation

Exam pearl:
Productive cough ≥3 months/year for 2 consecutive years = Chronic bronchitis.

Pathology-04.question: ১০) Bronchiectasis usually affects which of the following area of the lung?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is right and left lower lobes. Bronchiectasis commonly affects the lower lobes of both lungs, particularly the basal segments, due to impaired mucus clearance and gravitational pooling of secretions.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Left upper lobe – Can be involved, especially in post-tuberculous bronchiectasis, but is not the usual site.

  • Right middle lobe – Classically involved in middle lobe syndrome, but not the commonest site of bronchiectasis.

  • Left lower lobe – May be affected, but bronchiectasis usually involves both lower lobes.

High-yield points:

Bronchiectasis:

  • Site → Lower lobes (bilateral, especially basal segments)

  • Pathology → Irreversible bronchial dilatation

  • Common causes:

    • Previous severe infection

    • Cystic fibrosis

    • Primary ciliary dyskinesia

    • ABPA

Exam pearl:
Bronchiectasis = bilateral lower lobes (basal segments).

Pathology-04.question: ১১) Which of the following are the key inflammatory cells in B. asthma?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is eosinophils. Bronchial asthma is classically associated with eosinophilic airway inflammation, especially in allergic (Type 2) asthma. Eosinophils release inflammatory mediators that contribute to airway hyperresponsiveness and bronchial inflammation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neutrophils – Predominant in some severe asthma phenotypes and infection-related inflammation, but not the classic inflammatory cell.

  • Lymphocytes – Th2 lymphocytes play an important role by releasing cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13), but eosinophils are the key effector cells.

  • Basophils – Involved in allergic responses but are not the main inflammatory cells in asthma.

High-yield points:

Asthma inflammation:

  • Key cells → Eosinophils

  • Cytokines → IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (Th2 response)

  • Mediators → Histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins

Exam pearl:
Bronchial asthma = Eosinophilic inflammation.

Pathology-04.question: ১২) Right-to-left shunts occur in which of the following?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Eisenmenger syndrome. A right-to-left shunt occurs when a longstanding left-to-right shunt (e.g., ASD, VSD, PDA) causes pulmonary vascular remodeling, leading to pulmonary hypertension and reversal of shunt direction.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ASD – Usually causes a left-to-right shunt (oxygenated blood flows from LA → RA).

  • VSD – Initially causes a left-to-right shunt (LV → RV).

  • PDA – Usually causes a left-to-right shunt (aorta → pulmonary artery).

High-yield points:

Congenital heart shunts:

Condition Initial shunt
ASD Left → Right
VSD Left → Right
PDA Left → Right
Eisenmenger syndrome Right → Left

Eisenmenger features:

  • Pulmonary hypertension

  • Cyanosis

  • Clubbing

  • Reversal of shunt

Exam pearl:
Right-to-left shunt in congenital heart disease = Eisenmenger syndrome.

Pathology-04.question: ১৩) Chronic rheumatic heart disease is usually affecting which of the following heart valve?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is mitral valve. Chronic rheumatic heart disease most commonly affects the mitral valve, leading to mitral stenosis due to progressive fibrosis, leaflet thickening, and commissural fusion.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Aortic valve – The second most commonly affected valve, often with aortic regurgitation or stenosis.

  • Pulmonary valve – Rarely involved in rheumatic heart disease.

  • Tricuspid valve – May be affected but usually along with mitral valve disease and less commonly.

High-yield points:

Rheumatic heart disease valve involvement:

  1. Mitral valve (most common)

  2. Aortic valve

  3. Tricuspid valve

  4. Pulmonary valve (rare)

Classic lesion:

  • Mitral stenosis

  • "Fish-mouth" appearance due to commissural fusion

Exam pearl:
Chronic rheumatic heart disease = Mitral valve involvement (most common).

Pathology-04.question: ১৪) Hypertensive heart disease is usually affecting which of the following heart chamber?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is left ventricle. Chronic systemic hypertension increases afterload against which the left ventricle must pump, leading to left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) as an adaptive response.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Right atrium – Mainly affected by systemic venous pressure problems, not systemic hypertension.

  • Right ventricle – Affected by pulmonary hypertension, not systemic arterial hypertension.

  • Left atrium – May enlarge secondary to LV dysfunction and mitral valve disease, but it is not the primary chamber affected.

High-yield points:

Hypertensive heart disease:

  • Primary change → Left ventricular hypertrophy

  • Type → Concentric LVH

  • Mechanism → Increased afterload → increased wall stress → myocardial hypertrophy

  • Complications:

    • Heart failure

    • Arrhythmia

    • Ischaemic heart disease

Exam pearl:
Systemic hypertension → Left ventricular hypertrophy.

Pathology-04.question: ১৫) Which type of mutation occurs in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is autosomal dominant. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is most commonly caused by mutations in genes encoding sarcomere proteins, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

The most common affected genes include:

  • MYH7 → β-myosin heavy chain

  • MYBPC3 → myosin-binding protein C

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Autosomal recessive – Not the usual inheritance pattern for HCM.

  • X-linked dominant – Seen in some disorders but not typical for HCM.

  • X-linked recessive – Not associated with classic familial HCM.

High-yield points:

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy:

  • Inheritance → Autosomal dominant

  • Defect → Sarcomere protein mutation

  • Main feature → Left ventricular hypertrophy (often septal)

  • Complication → Sudden cardiac death, especially in young athletes

Exam pearl:
HCM = Autosomal dominant sarcomere mutation.

Pathology-04.question: ১৬) Transudative pleural effusion occurs in which of the following condition?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is cardiac failure. Transudative pleural effusion occurs due to an imbalance in hydrostatic and oncotic pressures, most commonly due to congestive heart failure causing increased pulmonary venous pressure.

The other options are incorrect because they usually cause exudative pleural effusion:

  • Malignancy → Exudative effusion due to increased vascular permeability or lymphatic obstruction.

  • Tuberculosis → Exudative effusion due to inflammatory pleural involvement.

  • Pneumonia → Exudative parapneumonic effusion due to infection and inflammation.

High-yield points:

Transudate causes (Think: pressure problem):

  • Heart failure (most common)

  • Cirrhosis

  • Nephrotic syndrome

  • Hypoalbuminaemia

Exudate causes (Think: inflammation/injury):

  • Pneumonia

  • Tuberculosis

  • Malignancy

  • Pulmonary embolism

Light’s criteria (Exudate if any present):

  • Pleural protein/serum protein >0.5

  • Pleural LDH/serum LDH >0.6

  • Pleural LDH > two-thirds upper normal serum LDH

Exam pearl:
Transudative pleural effusion = Cardiac failure.

Pathology-04.question: ১৭) Acute type-1 respiratory failure occurs in which of the following condition?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is pneumonia. Acute type 1 respiratory failure (hypoxaemic respiratory failure) occurs due to failure of oxygenation, usually from ventilation–perfusion mismatch or alveolar filling, as seen in pneumonia.

In pneumonia, inflammatory exudate fills alveoli, causing impaired oxygen diffusion and low PaO₂ with usually normal or low PaCO₂.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • COPD – Typically causes type 2 respiratory failure (hypercapnic) due to alveolar hypoventilation.

  • Lung fibrosis – Causes chronic restrictive lung disease and may cause type 1 respiratory failure, but it is usually chronic, not acute.

  • Right-to-left shunts – Can cause severe hypoxaemia, but are not the typical cause of acute type 1 respiratory failure in this context.

High-yield points:

Type 1 respiratory failure (Hypoxaemic):

  • PaO₂ ↓

  • PaCO₂ normal or ↓

  • Causes:

    • Pneumonia

    • Pulmonary oedema

    • ARDS

    • Pulmonary embolism

Type 2 respiratory failure (Hypercapnic):

  • PaO₂ ↓

  • PaCO₂ ↑

  • Causes:

    • COPD

    • Neuromuscular disease

    • Severe airway obstruction

Exam pearl:
Acute type 1 respiratory failure = Pneumonia (common cause).

Pathology-04.question: ১৮) Which of the following immunoglobulin is greatly associated with B.asthma?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is IgE. Bronchial asthma (especially allergic asthma) is strongly associated with IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity. Allergens stimulate Th2 cells, which promote B-cell class switching to IgE. IgE binds to mast cells and triggers release of inflammatory mediators causing bronchoconstriction.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • IgA – Important in mucosal immunity, especially respiratory secretions, but not the main immunoglobulin in asthma.

  • IgG – Involved in systemic immune responses and some hypersensitivity reactions, but not the classic mediator of asthma.

  • IgM – First antibody produced during primary immune response; not associated with allergic asthma.

High-yield points:

Allergic bronchial asthma:

  • Hypersensitivity type → Type I (immediate hypersensitivity)

  • Immunoglobulin → IgE

  • Main cells → Mast cells, eosinophils, Th2 lymphocytes

  • Key cytokines → IL-4, IL-5, IL-13

Exam pearl:
Bronchial asthma + allergy = IgE-mediated reaction.

Pathology-04.question: ১৯) In Urine R/M/E, WBC & nitrite is strongly suggestive of
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is UTI (urinary tract infection). The presence of increased WBCs (pyuria) and positive nitrite test in urine routine microscopy strongly suggests a bacterial UTI, especially due to Gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bladder carcinoma – May cause haematuria, but WBCs and nitrite positivity are not typical findings.

  • AGN (Acute glomerulonephritis) – Characteristically shows haematuria, RBC casts, and proteinuria, not nitrite positivity.

  • NS (Nephrotic syndrome) – Shows heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and oedema.

High-yield points:

Urine findings:

  • WBCs (pyuria) + nitrite positive → UTI

  • Nitrite positive → Nitrate-reducing bacteria (commonly E. coli)

  • RBC casts → Glomerulonephritis

  • Heavy proteinuria → Nephrotic syndrome

Exam pearl:
Pyuria + nitrite positivity = Bacterial UTI.

Pathology-04.question: ২০) In PBF: Oval macrocytosis, red cell fragmentation, neutrophil hypersegmentation are suggestive of which of the following?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is megaloblastic anaemia. Peripheral blood film (PBF) findings of macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils are classic features of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency causing megaloblastic anaemia.

Red cell fragmentation (schistocytes) may occasionally be seen due to ineffective erythropoiesis, but the key diagnostic findings are macro-ovalocytosis and neutrophil hypersegmentation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Iron deficiency anaemia – Shows microcytic hypochromic cells, pencil cells, and increased RDW.

  • Hemolysis – Shows schistocytes (in microangiopathic haemolysis), spherocytes, polychromasia, and reticulocytosis.

  • Sideroblastic anaemia – Shows dimorphic red cells and ring sideroblasts in bone marrow.

High-yield points:

Megaloblastic anaemia PBF:

  • Macro-ovalocytes

  • Hypersegmented neutrophils

  • Anisopoikilocytosis

  • ↑ MCV

Causes:

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency

  • Folate deficiency

Exam pearl:
Macro-ovalocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils = Megaloblastic anaemia.

Pathology-04.question: ২১) Which type of hypersensitivity reaction occurs in tuberculosis?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Type IV hypersensitivity. Tuberculosis causes a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T lymphocytes (especially Th1 cells) rather than antibodies.

In TB, sensitised T cells release cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ) that activate macrophages and produce granuloma formation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Type I – IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity (e.g., asthma, anaphylaxis).

  • Type II – Antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction (e.g., autoimmune haemolytic anaemia).

  • Type III – Immune complex-mediated reaction (e.g., serum sickness, SLE).

High-yield points:

Type Mechanism Example
I IgE + mast cells Asthma, anaphylaxis
II IgG/IgM against cell antigens Autoimmune haemolysis
III Immune complexes SLE
IV T-cell mediated Tuberculosis, Mantoux test

Exam pearl:
Tuberculosis = Type IV (delayed T-cell mediated hypersensitivity).

Pathology-04.question: ২২) Orthotolidine test is used to detect which of the following constituents in urine?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is RBC (blood) detection. Orthotolidine test is a chemical test used for detecting haemoglobin (occult blood) in urine, indicating the presence of red blood cells (RBCs).

The test is based on the peroxidase activity of haemoglobin, which causes oxidation of orthotolidine producing a colour change.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Sugar – Detected by tests such as Benedict’s test or glucose oxidase dipstick.

  • Ketone body – Detected by Rothera’s test or nitroprusside reaction.

  • pH – Detected by indicator strips.

High-yield points:

Urine chemical tests:

Test Detects
Orthotolidine test Blood/haemoglobin (RBCs)
Benedict’s test Reducing sugar
Rothera’s test Ketone bodies
Dipstick pH, glucose, protein, blood

Exam pearl:
Orthotolidine → Occult blood in urine.

Pathology-04.question: ২৩) Which of the following is pathognomonic for acute rheumatic fever?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Aschoff nodules. Aschoff bodies (Aschoff nodules) are the pathognomonic histological lesion of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). They consist of inflammatory cells, including Anitschkow cells (caterpillar-shaped nuclei), found mainly in the myocardium.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Carditis – A major Jones criterion of ARF but not pathognomonic.

  • Erythema (erythema marginatum) – A major Jones criterion but not pathognomonic.

  • Polyarthritis – The most common major Jones criterion, but not specific.

High-yield points:

Acute rheumatic fever (Jones criteria):

Major criteria:

  • Carditis

  • Migratory polyarthritis

  • Sydenham chorea

  • Erythema marginatum

  • Subcutaneous nodules

Pathognomonic finding:

  • Aschoff bodies in myocardium

Exam pearl:
Acute rheumatic fever → Aschoff nodules = pathognomonic.

Pathology-04.question: ২৪) Which of the following is the most common cause of coronary artery disease?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is atherosclerosis. The most common underlying cause of coronary artery disease (CAD) is atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries due to formation of atherosclerotic plaques, causing reduced myocardial blood supply.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thrombosis – Usually occurs as a complication of atherosclerotic plaque rupture and can cause acute coronary syndrome.

  • Hypertension (HTN) – A major risk factor for CAD but not the direct cause.

  • Diabetes mellitus (DM) – A major risk factor that accelerates atherosclerosis.

High-yield points:

Coronary artery disease:

  • Most common cause → Atherosclerosis

  • Major risk factors:

    • Smoking

    • Hypertension

    • Diabetes mellitus

    • Dyslipidaemia

    • Increasing age

Exam pearl:
CAD = Atherosclerotic plaque in coronary arteries.

Pathology-04.question: ২৫) Which of the following is the most common congenital heart disease?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is ventricular septal defect (VSD). VSD is the most common congenital heart disease overall. It results in an abnormal communication between the right and left ventricles, usually producing a left-to-right shunt.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ASD – A common congenital heart defect but less frequent than VSD.

  • PDA – Common in premature infants but not the most common congenital heart disease overall.

  • TOF (Tetralogy of Fallot) – The most common cyanotic congenital heart disease, but not the most common congenital heart disease overall.

High-yield points:

Congenital heart disease:

  • Most common overall → VSD

  • Most common cyanotic CHD → Tetralogy of Fallot

  • Most common acyanotic CHD → VSD

Exam pearl:
CHD (overall) = VSD; Cyanotic CHD = TOF.

Pathology-04.question: ২৬) Which organism is responsible for developing penumonia in a chronic alcholic person?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Klebsiella pneumoniae. Chronic alcoholism is a classic risk factor for Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia due to impaired host defence mechanisms. It commonly causes severe lobar pneumonia with "currant jelly" sputum.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neisseria – Not a typical cause of pneumonia in alcoholics.

  • Legionella – Causes atypical pneumonia, often associated with contaminated water exposure and hyponatraemia.

  • Pseudomonas – Associated with hospital-acquired pneumonia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, bronchiectasis, and cystic fibrosis.

High-yield points:

Risk factors and organisms:

Pathology-04.question: ২৭) Which of the following is most important risk factor for lung cancer?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is smoking. Cigarette smoking is the most important risk factor for lung cancer, responsible for the majority of lung cancer cases. The risk increases with the number of pack-years smoked.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Genetic predisposition – Can increase susceptibility but contributes less than smoking.

  • Air pollutant – A recognized risk factor, especially in occupational and environmental exposures, but less important than smoking.

  • Atopy – Associated with allergic diseases such as asthma, not lung cancer.

High-yield points:

Risk factors for lung cancer:

  1. Smoking (major risk factor)

  2. Occupational exposure:

    • Asbestos

    • Radon

    • Arsenic

    • Chromium

  3. Air pollution

  4. Genetic susceptibility

Smoking associations:

  • Squamous cell carcinoma

  • Small cell carcinoma

Exam pearl:
Most important risk factor for lung cancer = Smoking.

Pathology-04.question: ২৮) Which of the following is the most important modifiable risk factor of coronary artery disease?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is smoking. Smoking is the most important modifiable risk factor for coronary artery disease (CAD). It accelerates atherosclerosis, promotes endothelial dysfunction, increases platelet aggregation, and reduces oxygen delivery due to carbon monoxide exposure.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Obesity – A modifiable risk factor, but its effect is often mediated through hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidaemia.

  • Hypertension (HTN) – A major risk factor for CAD, but smoking has a stronger independent association with premature coronary events.

  • Diabetes mellitus (DM) – A powerful risk factor and considered a CAD risk equivalent, but not the most important modifiable factor.

High-yield points:

Major modifiable CAD risk factors:

  1. Smoking (most important preventable risk factor)

  2. Hypertension

  3. Dyslipidaemia (↑ LDL cholesterol)

  4. Diabetes mellitus

  5. Obesity and physical inactivity

Exam pearl:
Most important modifiable risk factor for CAD = Smoking.

Pathology-04.question: ২৯) Primary cardiac tumor(myxoma) is usually occuring which of the following area?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is left atrium. Cardiac myxoma, the most common primary benign cardiac tumour, occurs most commonly in the left atrium (about 75% of cases). It usually arises from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Right atrium – Less common site (about 15–20%).

  • Right ventricle – Rarely affected.

  • Left ventricle – Rarely affected.

High-yield points:

Cardiac myxoma:

  • Most common primary cardiac tumour

  • Site → Left atrium

  • Origin → Interatrial septum (fossa ovalis)

  • Symptoms:

    • Obstructive symptoms (mimics mitral stenosis)

    • Embolic events

    • Constitutional symptoms (IL-6 mediated)

Exam pearl:
Myxoma = Left atrium + fossa ovalis.

Pathology-04.question: ৩০) Both ESR & CRP raised in which of the following condition?
Pathology-04.exp:
The correct answer is acute inflammatory diseases. Both ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein) are inflammatory markers that rise in acute inflammation due to increased production of acute-phase proteins.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Multiple myeloma – Causes a markedly raised ESR due to increased immunoglobulins (rouleaux formation), but CRP may be normal or only mildly raised unless there is associated inflammation.

  • Pregnancy – ESR is increased due to raised fibrinogen levels, but CRP is usually normal.

  • Old age – ESR may increase slightly, but CRP is not typically elevated.

High-yield points:

ESR vs CRP:

Feature ESR CRP
